h1: Choosing a colour palette for a brewery that works on cans and taps
title: Choosing a Brewery Colour Palette | Craft Beer School
desc: How to choose brewery brand colours that hold up on printed cans, sleeves, tap handles, signage and phone screens, with practical tests for each.
teaser: A colour that sings on a screen can turn muddy on aluminium. Pick your palette where it will actually live.
standfirst: A brewery's colours have to survive metal cans, paper labels, wooden tap handles, a sunlit menu board and a phone screen. Here is how we choose a palette that holds together across all of them.
sections: Start from where the colours will live

Most palettes are chosen on a monitor and then forced onto everything else. Do it the other way round. List every surface your brand touches: printed cans or sleeves, keg collars, tap handles or tap labels, the taproom wall, menus, merchandise, Instagram. Each one reproduces colour differently.

Aluminium is the hardest. Ink printed directly on a can sits on silver metal unless the printer lays down a white base first. Without that base, colours look darker and cooler. Pale tints can almost vanish. Ask your can or sleeve supplier how they print before you fall for a pastel.

• One or two core colours. These carry the brand on every surface. Choose colours that still read in a single-colour print, because some keg collars and stamps will only allow one.
  • A neutral. A near-black, cream or off-white for text and backgrounds.
  • A range set. A family of colours for individual beers, so the core range is easy to tell apart.

Keep the range set disciplined. If every new seasonal gets a fresh colour chosen in isolation, the shelf looks like several breweries. Decide in advance which colours belong to the core beers and which are kept for limited releases. Our guide to modular identity systems goes further into this.

Write each colour down in every system you will need: a Pantone or spot reference for printing, CMYK for process print, RGB and hex for screens. A printer in Pune and a signage shop in Hyderabad will both get closer if they have a physical swatch and the same reference. Without that, every supplier "matches" by eye and the brand drifts.

Ask for a printed proof on the actual material for each important application. A colour proof on paper says little about how a sleeve will look over metal.

Drinkers read colour as a flavour cue. Greens and yellows tend to suggest hops and citrus, deep browns and black suggest roast, pinks and reds suggest fruit. You can break these habits on purpose, but know when you are doing it. A black can for a light lager will confuse more shoppers than it intrigues.

Indian shelves add their own cues. Many mass-market beer brands own strong reds, greens and golds. A craft palette that sits too close to a big brand's colours may look like an imitation rather than an alternative.

Every colour pair you plan to put text on needs enough contrast to read in poor light. Check text and background pairs with a contrast checker for screens, then test print. Yellow text on white and red text on black both fail more often than designers expect. On a tap handle, the beer name must be readable from the far end of the bar.

A small taproom detail: tap lists are often viewed under warm amber lighting. Warm light flattens reds and oranges and makes some blues look grey. Hold your tap labels under the bar's actual lights before you print a full set.
Keeping it consistent as the range grows

The palette is easy to hold in the first year with four beers. It falls apart in year three, when there are twelve beers, two collaborations and a festival special designed in a hurry by whoever was free. Write the rules down while they are fresh: which colours belong to which beers, which are never used for text, how much of a can face the core colour must cover.

Put those rules in the brand book and send them with every design brief. Then keep one physical reference set of printed cans and labels in the office. When a new supplier says their print is a match, hold it next to the reference rather than a screen. That habit costs nothing and catches most drift before it reaches the shelf.

1. Print the palette on a can sleeve proof, a paper label and a tap label.
  2. Look at them under daylight, fridge LED and warm bar light.
  3. Photograph them on a phone and compare with your screen version.
  4. Print the core colour in one colour only, as a stamp would. Check it still looks like you.

Colour is the first decision a shopper notices and the last one a brewery usually tests. Getting it right on every material, at a price you can repeat, is a packaging problem as much as a design one.
faqs: How many colours should a brewery brand have?
Usually one or two core colours, a neutral and a separate range set for individual beers. More than that and the brand gets hard to recognise.
Why does my colour look different on the can?
Ink on aluminium sits over silver metal unless a white base is printed first, which darkens and cools most colours. Ask for a proof on the real can or sleeve.
If you print with more than one supplier, yes. A shared spot reference and a physical swatch keep cans, signs and merchandise from drifting apart.
